Quick aside, I have a strange scientific background. My dissertation was geochem and paleoclimatology. When I joined a major oil company I started working doing paleoclimatic reconstructions, but that has shifted to a lot of geophysics and managerial bullshit.

Back to the topic. Climate in the US is dominated by two air movements. The Intertropical Convergence Zone (southern current that flows East to west) and the Jet Stream (northern current that flows west to east). Look up Hadley Cells on Wiki to get a better idea. Their locations are based on the thermal gradient from the pole to the equator. When it's colder these shift to the south. This supplies much of the South West with air sourced from the Pacific (west to east). When this air hits the Rockies it rains out and leaves little moisture for the continent.

When it's warmer these air currents shift northwards. This causes the Gulf of Mexico to be the moisture source. Since there are no mountains in Texas, the moisture can travel farther inland. You can look at precipitation amounts by monthly average at NOAA to see the effect.

Liberals electoral reform plan is legally futile

The only problem with Roth and Roth's premise is that it's fundamentally wrong.

National debate is raging over the Liberal government’s plan to reform Canada’s electoral system without a referendum. A slap in the face to voters, many have said. But the voters can be ignored, at least until 2019. More problematic for the Liberals: Their plan is also a slap in the face to the Supreme Court of Canada, which less than two years ago reiterated that fundamental constitutional reform can proceed only with broad provincial consensus.

No matter how much they may want it to be, changing the electoral system is not a "fundamental constitution reform" unless it changes what the constitution says about elections and voting.

Section 3 of the Charter of Rights says

Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of the members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly and to be qualified for membership therein.

That's not being changed.

Section 4 says

4.(1) No House of Commons and no legislative assembly shall continue for longer than five years from the date fixed for the return of the writs at a general election of its members.

(2) In time of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection, a House of Commons may be continued by Parliament and a legislative assembly may be continued by the legislature beyond five years if such continuation is not opposed by the votes of more than one-third of the members of the House of Commons or the legislative assembly, as the case may be.

That's not being changed either.

..... and unfortunately for Roth and Roth that pretty well wraps up what the constitution says about elections and voting.
